plan: [This is a common-value auction with winner’s curse. My signal is 24; unconditional E[common|signal=24]=24.5, but conditioning on being the highest (beating two rivals) reduces the expected common value. Solving for E[common | my signal=24 and others’ signals ≤24] gives ≈23.82. In a symmetric equilibrium of the second-price auction I should bid that conditional expectation. I therefore shade slightly below my signal to avoid the winner’s curse.]

[I will bid the expected common value conditional on my signal and on being the highest (to avoid the winner's curse). With s=27, E[C|s]=24.5. Conditioning on others' signals ≤27 gives posterior weight ∝(47−c)^2 on c∈[20,29], yielding E[C | win,s=27] ≈ 23.91. In a second‑price auction the equilibrium bid equals this conditional expectation, so I round to the nearest $0.1 and bid 23.9.]

[My observed signal S=15 gives no information about the common value C beyond the prior (C uniform 20–29), so E[C|S]=24.5. In a second-price auction with common value uncertainty, a good practical rule is to bid near the posterior mean but shade downward to reduce winner’s curse risk. I therefore choose a conservative bid slightly below 24.5 to maximize long-run expected profit while avoiding overpayment.]
